explanations.answer: The ark of the covenant of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Solomon, Israel's king, calls in all the leaders to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Zion, the City of David (1 Kings 8:1). You don't call every tribal head and family leader in Israel for a small errand. When that many people show up, something BIG is getting carried.

explanations.answer: The bronze serpent that Moses made
explanations.explanation: Good memory, because Moses, Israel's leader, really did make a bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9). But this passage doesn't bring it up at all. Solomon gathers the leaders to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD (1 Kings 8:1). Right story, different shiny object.

explanations.answer: The sword that belonged to Goliath
explanations.explanation: Goliath, the giant David defeated, had a sword that people remember (1 Samuel 17:51). It isn't what Solomon's leaders gather for, though. The text says they're there to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Zion (1 Kings 8:1). I'd have loved to see a giant's sword carried up the street, but that's a different day.

I see why you'd say that, since Solomon is the king and he's running the whole show. But the text says something different. When all the elders have arrived, the priests take up the ark (1 Kings 8:3). Solomon gathers everyone, and the priests do the lifting.

Right, friend. The king calls everybody together, but he doesn't pick up the ark himself. Once all the elders have arrived, the priests take it up (1 Kings 8:3). Even a king has a spot in the line, and mine is usually behind the cookie tray.

explanations.answer: So many they could not be counted
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Solomon and the whole congregation sacrifice so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered (1 Kings 8:5). Somebody started counting and gave up, I bet. I once lost track counting a single batch of sprinkles.

That sounds nice and tidy, but the text doesn't give a number like that. It says the sheep and oxen were so many that they could not be counted or numbered (1 Kings 8:5). A tidy count would have been easy to write down. The text says nobody could count them.

explanations.answer: Seven of each and no more
explanations.explanation: Seven is a big number in the Bible, so I get the guess. But this verse doesn't say seven. It says the sheep and oxen were so many that they could not be counted or numbered (1 Kings 8:5). Seven of each is fourteen animals, and nobody loses count of fourteen.

explanations.answer: Overshadow the ark and its poles
explanations.explanation: You got it. The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and overshadow the ark and its poles (1 Kings 8:7). The priests set it down beneath those wings, in the Most Holy Place (1 Kings 8:6). It's like a big covering over the whole thing.

explanations.answer: Lift the ark up off the floor
explanations.explanation: I see the picture you had in mind. But the text doesn't say the wings lift anything. It says the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and overshadow the ark and its poles (1 Kings 8:7). The ark stays where the priests set it.

Good try, friend, but the text gives the wings a different job. The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and overshadow the ark and its poles (1 Kings 8:7). They're spread out over the ark, and the text says nothing about the doors.

That's what the text says. There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). The writer says it plainly, so I will too. Two tablets, and that's the whole list.

explanations.answer: The tablets and a jar of manna
explanations.explanation: Manna is the food God provided for Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16:4, 35), so I see why it came to mind. But this verse closes the door on extras. It says there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets (1 Kings 8:9). No jar of manna is in the count.

Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), is a name that comes up around the ark, so the guess makes sense. But 1 Kings 8:9 is clear. There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets. No staff on that list, friend.

That's right. Moses, Israel's leader, placed the tablets in the ark at Horeb, where the LORD had made a covenant with the Israelites after they came out of Egypt (1 Kings 8:9). Those tablets traveled a long way to reach this temple. I'd be worn out just hearing about it.
Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), is an easy name to land on. But the text names someone else here. It says Moses had placed the tablets in the ark at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). Moses is the one.

Joshua, Moses' attendant (Exodus 24:13), is a name that goes with Moses, so I understand the pick. But the text doesn't name him here. It says the two stone tablets were the ones Moses had placed in the ark at Horeb (1 Kings 8:9). Moses did the placing.

That's right, friend. The cloud fills the house of the LORD so that the priests could not stand there to minister (1 Kings 8:11). These are the priests who just carried the ark in, and now they can't even stand there to do their work. That tells me something big is happening.

I can see why you'd doubt it, but the text says it outright. The cloud filled the house of the LORD so that the priests could not stand there to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11). The priests had just come out of the Holy Place, and then the cloud filled the house. So the statement on this card is true.

Yes. The text says the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud (1 Kings 8:11). Then it says, "For the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 8:11). The blank is glory.

The word of the LORD matters all through this story, so I get the pick. But this verse says something else filled the house. It says, "For the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 8:11). The blank is glory.

I understand the guess, because the priests could not stand there to minister. But the text doesn't mention fear here. It says, "For the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD." (1 Kings 8:11). I'd only be guessing about how they felt, and the text gives us glory.

explanations.answer: A place for You to dwell forever
explanations.explanation: That's it. Solomon says to the LORD, "I have indeed built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever." (1 Kings 8:13). He says it right after the cloud fills the house. Forever is the word he uses, friend.

explanations.answer: A place for You to visit yearly
explanations.explanation: A yearly visit would be easy to plan, like a family reunion. But Solomon doesn't say that to the LORD. He says it's "…a place for You to dwell forever." (1 Kings 8:13). Dwelling is a lot more than visiting.

explanations.answer: A place for You to rest awhile
explanations.explanation: That one sounds cozy, but it isn't what Solomon says. He calls the house "…a place for You to dwell forever." (1 Kings 8:13). Forever is a lot longer than awhile, friend.

I see why you'd say that, since the elders are named right at the start of the passage (1 Kings 8:1). But the text says Solomon blesses everybody. With the whole assembly of Israel standing there, the king turned around and blessed them all (1 Kings 8:14). Nobody gets left out of that blessing.

That's right. The text says, "…the king turned around and blessed them all" (1 Kings 8:14). The whole assembly of Israel is standing there, and the blessing goes to every one of them. No VIP section, friend.

That's right. Solomon quotes God as saying, "Since the day I brought My people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel in which to build a house so that My Name would be there." (1 Kings 8:16). That's a long stretch of days with no city chosen. Then God turns to someone else, and that's coming up.

I understand the doubt, but the statement on this card matches the text. Solomon quotes God as saying that since the day He brought Israel out of Egypt, He had not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel to build a house so that His Name would be there (1 Kings 8:16). So the card is true. In the same verse God says, "But I have chosen David to be over My people Israel." (1 Kings 8:16).
That's right. God says, "But I have chosen David to be over My people Israel." (1 Kings 8:16). No city was chosen, but a man was. Solomon is quoting what God told his own father.

Saul, made king at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15), is a name people reach for, so I understand the guess. But the verse names someone else. God says, "But I have chosen David to be over My people Israel." (1 Kings 8:16).

Samuel, a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), is a well-known name in Israel's story. But this verse names someone else. God says, "But I have chosen David to be over My people Israel." (1 Kings 8:16). David is the one.

explanations.answer: He did well to have it in his heart
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says to David, "Since it was in your heart to build a house for My Name, you have done well to have this in your heart." (1 Kings 8:18). David doesn't get to build it, but the LORD still says he did well. I think that's a kind thing to hear.

explanations.answer: He never should have thought of it
explanations.explanation: That's not what the LORD says. He says, "Since it was in your heart to build a house for My Name, you have done well to have this in your heart." (1 Kings 8:18). It's the opposite of a scolding. He says David did well.

explanations.answer: He must wait until he is much older
explanations.explanation: A waiting period would make sense on a calendar. But the LORD doesn't mention David's age. He says it was good that this was in David's heart, and then He says David is not the one to build it (1 Kings 8:18-19). Waiting isn't part of the answer.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "…your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name." (1 Kings 8:19). And Solomon, speaking as David's son, says he has built it (1 Kings 8:20). The house David wanted to build got built by his own son.
That's not the word the LORD uses. He says, "…your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name." (1 Kings 8:19). It's David's own son, and that's Solomon.

A servant could build something, but that's not what the LORD says. He tells David, "…your son, your own offspring, will build the house for My Name." (1 Kings 8:19). The word is son. Solomon is that son.

That's it. Solomon says the ark contains the covenant of the LORD that He made with "…our fathers when He brought them out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 8:21). The ark holds that covenant, and the tablets are inside it (1 Kings 8:9). That's a long way from Egypt to this temple.

Kings are a reasonable guess with a king speaking. But Solomon says something else. He says the covenant was made with "…our fathers when He brought them out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 8:21). The fathers are the ones he names, friend.

The priests and Levites do carry the ark in this story (1 Kings 8:4), so I get why they came to mind. But that isn't who Solomon names here. He says the LORD made the covenant with "…our fathers when He brought them out of the land of Egypt." (1 Kings 8:21). The fathers are the answer.
